# Results — Study 476 (TD Sequential — DeMark 9-13)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The believers' claim — **a
completed TD Buy Setup (9 consecutive closes below close-4) and Countdown (13) marks exhaustion
of the down-move, a high-probability long** — encoded as a mechanical rule. A setup-9 long fires
on the bar completing nine consecutive closes each below the close four bars earlier; a
countdown-13 long fires on the bar completing thirteen "close ≤ low two bars earlier" rungs after
a setup. Entry is the **next close** (one documented lag); we measure the forward 5/10/20/60-day
return. Offline & deterministic once cached; run `python examples/verify.py` to reproduce.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily adjusted (**total-return**) closes for **SPY, QQQ, IWM, DIA, GLD** (public, no key) |
| Window | 2005-01-03 → 2026-05-29 (**As-of 2026-05-31**, partial June dropped; **21.4** years) |
| SPY fingerprint | `4cb5244f3990` (sha1[:12] of the close column, As-of slice) |
| Entries | **239** mechanical buy setup-9 completions pooled across the 5 tapes |
| Timing / costs | setup/countdown read on close of *t*; enter the **next close** (one lag); hold 5/10/20/60 days; **1 bp** one-way × 2 legs per signal |

> **Price-only vs total-return.** The ETFs are auto-adjusted (dividends reinvested) — labelled
> total-return everywhere. The Signal axis uses a basket of **surviving** liquid ETFs; this is a
> single-instrument timing study, not a cross-sectional anomaly, so survivorship affects only the
> drift baseline (which is exactly what the random-entry control neutralizes).

## The signal — buy setup-9 vs a drift-matched random baseline (the honest test)

One-sample *t* is the **misleading** number (it measures the index's upward drift); the
**setup-vs-random** comparison is the test that matters. Δ = setup − random. The Welch column
below uses a **single** random draw (seed 7) — read it together with the seed-robustness note,
which is decisive.

| horizon | n | setup | win% | one-sample *t* | random | Δ (setup−random) | net of cost | Welch *t* (seed 7) | *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 5-day  | 239 | +55.0 bps | 55% | +2.21 | +6.2 bps | **+48.9 bps** | +53.0 bps | +1.76 | 0.080 |
| 10-day | 239 | +42.9 bps | 56% | +1.55 | +54.0 bps | **−11.1 bps** | +40.9 bps | −0.32 | 0.751 |
| 20-day | 239 | +193.4 bps | 67% | +5.08 | +51.0 bps | **+142.4 bps** | +191.4 bps | +2.91 | 0.004 |
| 60-day | 234 | +371.6 bps | 70% | +5.32 | +100.8 bps | **+270.8 bps** | +369.6 bps | +3.31 | 0.001 |

At first glance the 20d/60d Welch *t* (+2.91 / +3.31) clear the desk's *t* ≥ 2 bar — a rare
near-hit for a chart rule. **But that single Welch number is an artifact of the lucky random
seed.** Re-running the random baseline over **200 fresh draws** and comparing the setup mean to
the *distribution* of random-baseline means gives the honest empirical *p*:

| horizon | setup | random (avg of 200 draws) | Δ | empirical *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 5-day  | +55.0 bps | +27.9 bps | +27.2 bps | 0.139 |
| 10-day | +42.9 bps | +49.6 bps | −6.7 bps | 0.582 |
| 20-day | +193.4 bps | +102.4 bps | **+91.0 bps** | **0.060** |
| 60-day | +371.6 bps | +302.0 bps | +69.6 bps | 0.204 |

Averaged over seeds the setup-vs-random Welch *t* at 20d is **+2.07** (range −0.00…+5.61) and at
60d is **+0.82** (range −1.09…+3.31) — it straddles the bar at 20d and fails it at 60d. The
empirical *p* never clears 0.05 (closest is **0.060** at 20d). So there is a *hint* of an edge
near 20 days, but it does **not** survive a properly sampled random baseline. Most of the
spectacular one-sample *t* (20d +5.08, 60d +5.32) is the usual **beta** — long-only entries on
an up-drifting tape.

## Countdown-13 vs random baseline (pooled)

DeMark's deeper "13" exhaustion signal is **weaker**, not stronger, than the 9:

| horizon | n | countdown | win% | one-sample *t* | random | Δ | Welch *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 5-day  | 183 | +1.5 bps | 55% | +0.05 | +16.2 bps | −14.7 bps | −0.51 |
| 10-day | 180 | +20.7 bps | 49% | +0.63 | −26.5 bps | +47.2 bps | +1.30 |
| 20-day | 180 | +38.1 bps | 56% | +1.00 | −84.2 bps | +122.3 bps | +2.36 |
| 60-day | 180 | +282.1 bps | 64% | +3.80 | +156.5 bps | +125.6 bps | +1.51 |

The "13" — the count DeMark sells as the *strongest* exhaustion read — does worse than the "9"
at short horizons and never clears *t* ≥ 2 robustly. If the count truly forecast exhaustion, the
deeper 13 should be the better signal; it isn't.

## Per-ticker (H = 20) — positive everywhere, but that's the drift

| ticker | entries | setup | one-sample *t* | random | Δ (setup−random) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY | 40 | +87.9 bps | +1.21 | +39.3 bps | +48.6 bps |
| QQQ | 43 | +273.4 bps | +2.31 | +88.2 bps | +185.3 bps |
| IWM | 43 | +297.5 bps | +2.92 | +2.7 bps | +294.9 bps |
| DIA | 50 | +133.3 bps | +1.83 | +33.7 bps | +99.6 bps |
| GLD | 63 | +182.5 bps | +3.41 | +83.4 bps | +99.1 bps |

The deltas are positive in all five names — but the per-ticker *n* is tiny (40–63 setups over 21
years), the random baseline here is again a single draw, and the pooled empirical *p* (0.060)
shows the aggregate doesn't reach significance. Consistent-sign-but-not-significant is the
fingerprint of a small drift tilt, not a forecast.

## Geometry placebo — scramble the count's lookback, nothing changes

The decisive "does the specific 4-bar count matter?" test: rebuild the buy setup with a
**permuted comparison offset** (2,3,5,6,7,8 — every plausible lookback *except* the canonical 4),
keeping the same 9-bar setup length and the same price marginal. If DeMark's exact 4-bar geometry
carried the information, the scramble should collapse the result.

| test | observed setup-9 20d return | placebo *p* | draws |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY scrambled-lookback setup | +87.9 bps | **0.673** | 500 |

**67% of scrambled-lookback setups match or beat the canonical 4-bar one** (*p* = 0.673). The
specific "close vs close four bars ago" count carries no special information — any down-streak
detector does as well. The "9-13 count forecasts exhaustion" mechanism is busted: whatever faint
20d tilt exists is generic "buy after a down-streak", not DeMark's geometry.

## Synthetic positive control — the harness CAN bank a real exhaustion bounce

On a deterministic tape with a *planted* post-setup reversal (knob `edge`), the same setup-9 rule
behaves exactly as it must — so the flat real-tape result is a genuine "nothing there", not a
dead detector.

| planted edge | n | setup | win% | one-sample *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **0.00** (no bounce) | 62 | +68.0 bps | 52% | +1.28 |
| **0.40** (real planted bounce) | 78 | +277.2 bps | 79% | **+6.55** |

With no planted bounce the control sits near the drift floor (*t* = +1.28, win 52%, no false
exhaustion edge); a real planted post-setup reversal lights up at *t* = +6.55 with a 79%
win-rate. The detector is live — so the failure on the real tape to clear the random baseline is
an honest null, not a broken pipeline.

## Verdict

- **Signal — WEAK.** The buy setup-9 *hints* at a 20-day edge over a drift-matched random
  baseline (Δ = +91 bps), but it does **not** survive a properly sampled baseline: empirical
  *p* = 0.060 at 20d (closest of all horizons) and the seed-averaged Welch *t* is only +2.07 at
  20d / +0.82 at 60d. The eye-catching single-seed Welch *t* (+2.91 / +3.31) and the one-sample
  *t* (+5.08 / +5.32) are mostly the index's upward drift. DeMark's deeper "13" is *weaker*, not
  stronger. A near-miss, not a confirmed signal.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** Whatever faint tilt exists is generic dip-buying drift, not a
  scalable edge; costs only deepen the hole and the 239 setups over 21 years (~11/yr) give no
  capacity. You'd capture the same drift more cheaply by holding the index.
- **"Does the 9-13 count forecast exhaustion?" — BUSTED.** The scrambled-lookback placebo leaves
  the result intact (*p* = 0.673): any down-streak detector does as well as DeMark's exact 4-bar
  count, and the "stronger" 13-countdown is the weaker signal. The specific 9-13 geometry carries
  no exhaustion information.
